repairs.value: Strongest feature: Sechler’s appeal to Lewis’s honest seekers addresses salvation without Christian vocabulary by distinguishing truth-oriented conduct from an explicit theological proposition. Principal limitation: The example makes inclusivist Christianity intelligible, but does not explain how sincere seeking constitutes service to God or when intellectual nonbelief remains culpable, matching evidential warrant of 63. Live burden: Sechler must specify why truth-seeking without doctrinal recognition suffices for salvation while Christian exclusivism remains meaningful, especially when Clifton asks whether punishment still turns on propositions someone cannot voluntarily find convincing. Locked score: The 76 reflects central relevance at 84 and direct engagement, while leaving the route from honest inquiry to salvation substantially less established than its plausibility framing suggests.

Strongest feature: Clifton turns Sechler’s proposal into a precise moral-justice test: whether requiring propositional belief punishes someone for involuntarily failing to find particular claims convincing. Principal limitation: The objection assumes the decisive Christian condition is assent to propositions, yet Sechler locates salvation in sincere truth-seeking, so Clifton needs to show this conduct-sensitive route ultimately restores the condemned belief requirement. Live burden: Clifton must distinguish blameless nonpersuasion from culpable resistance and demonstrate that Sechler’s Lewis-inspired seeker nevertheless faces punishment, rather than restating the broader problem of nonbelief. Locked score: The 83 fits responsiveness at 88 and central relevance at 89, while evidential warrant at 70 correctly registers unresolved dependence on what salvation actually requires.
